tldr: The thread opened Nov 4 with LooM, an arXiv method that stops memory growing with loop count in looped transformers; it shares only a name with the agent tool. On Nov 17 a Loom agent-memory project reached Hacker News, pitched as memory that keeps up with your code.
whats_new: A Nov 21 Hacker News post pitches Loom as one layer for shared agent memory, document search and code indexing, four days after a Loom post on agent memory that tracks code changes.
why_it_matters: Loom bundles three things agent stacks usually run separately (memory store, doc retrieval, code index), so adopting it means trusting one tool to keep all three in sync with a changing repo.

beats.headline: LooM paper: loop-invariant memory for looped transformers
beats.summary: A model-architecture paper on memory and compute in re-executed layers; unrelated to the agent tool.

beats.headline: Loom reaches Hacker News as agent memory that keeps up with your code
Loom pitched as shared memory plus document search plus code indexing
beats.summary: The scope widens from per-agent memory to a shared layer with retrieval and a code index.

open_questions: Are the Nov 17 and Nov 21 Hacker News posts the same Loom project, or two tools with the same name?
How does Loom keep its code index and memories current when files are renamed, refactored or deleted?
Does Loom define what happens when two agents write conflicting entries to shared memory?
Does Loom run locally, or does shared memory require a hosted backend?
take_for_builders: Before wiring Loom into an agent stack, test it on a repo mid-refactor: check that the code index and stored memories drop references to deleted or moved code.
